name: Castella
origin: Kasutera, brought to Nagasaki by 16th-century Portuguese traders (its name derives from Pão de Castela, 'bread of Castile') and adapted over centuries into a distinctly Japanese honey sponge, baked tall in a wooden frame.

ingredients.note: sugar fraction of honey (or mizuame starch syrup) at 10% of flour mass, split by USDA honey composition (~83% sugars, ~17% water)
an unusually egg-rich sponge, the real hallmark of castella's dense, moist, fine crumb
traditional castella relies almost entirely on the whipped-egg foam; a small baking-powder dose is common in modern recipes for reliability, modelled here as bicarbonate

process.name: whip eggs and sugar
process.description: whip whole eggs with sugar and honey to a thick, pale ribbon foam

process.name: fold in flour
process.description: fold in sifted flour and leavening in stages

process.name: bake
process.description: bake tall in a wooden or paper-lined frame at a moderate temperature so the crumb sets evenly without a crust forming too fast

notes: Egg mass at 180% of flour, with honey rather than only granulated sugar, is representative of published castella formulas; honey's real composition (USDA FoodData Central: ~82.4 g sugars, ~17.1 g water per 100 g) is split into its own sugar- and liquid-role lines. Little or no added fat is traditional and correct here — castella's richness comes entirely from egg, not butter or oil.
